passage: Tuesday, late. I froze again. Baljeet was alone at the canteen table, I walked over, and what came out of my mouth was "Did you finish the economics notes?" Notes! My ears were burning all the way to the hostel. I keep picturing her telling her friends and everyone laughing. First I thought of asking Kabir to find out what she thinks of me, or dropping hints in the class chat until she works it out. But that is just another way of never risking anything. A no would hurt, I know that. It would not make me a joke or a failure. So: Friday, after the seminar, one simple sentence. Would you like to get coffee sometime? Then whatever she says, I will have said it myself. My hands are still shaking as I write this. Lokesh

qa.q: What did Lokesh say to Baljeet in the canteen instead of what he wanted to say?
qa.a: He asked, "Did you finish the economics notes?"

qa.q: What is Lokesh afraid of, and how does he think about it by the end?
qa.a: He fears being laughed at if Baljeet says no. By the end he accepts that a no would hurt but would not make him a joke or a failure.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do on Friday, and why is it better than using Kabir?
qa.a: He can ask once, in one simple sentence. That keeps it honest and lets him hear her real answer instead of hiding behind a messenger.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see a direct invitation compared with hints or a message through Kabir?
qa.a: She would probably find a direct question easier to answer clearly and kindly than hints she has to decode or a message passed through a friend.

grounding: The diarist freezes from fear of humiliation and resolves to ask once, accepting a no would hurt but not define him.
